`case_study:franklin-templeton-debt-2020` | 2020-04-23 | tickers: - | confidence: verified

On 23 Apr 2020 Franklin Templeton MF froze and wound up six credit-oriented debt schemes (incl. Franklin India Credit Risk, Ultra Short Bond, Low Duration) with ~Rs 25,215 cr AUM, citing Covid-era illiquidity and redemption pressure. Investors were locked in; after a Supreme Court-supervised liquidation by SBI MF, unitholders ultimately received ~Rs 27,508 cr, i.e., >100% of AUM at closure -- but over ~3 years, with forced illiquidity at the worst time. Visible flags: (1) schemes held concentrated, low-rated or unrated papers and structured obligations (promoter-backed loans against shares, group holdcos) that had no secondary market; (2) yields well above category -- the extra yield was liquidity and credit risk; (3) earlier losses on Vodafone Idea and Essel group paper (2019-20) and side-pocketing; (4) the schemes had to borrow to meet redemptions in Mar-Apr 2020. SEBI later penalised Franklin and barred it from launching new debt schemes for two years (2021). Lesson: a debt fund's YTM above peers is a risk measure, not a reward; check portfolio liquidity, single-issuer exposure, unrated share and borrowing; even good recovery outcomes can come with years of lock-in.

**Lesson:** Extra yield = liquidity/credit risk
**Spotted early by:** fixed-income analysts tracking portfolio disclosures
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:avoid-ruin`

body: `insight:rerating-phases-end` · confidence: unverified Indian sector bull runs often get most of their return from multiple expansion, not earnings. When that happens, the next decade's return is borrowed. Examples: capital goods (2003–Jan 2008 at P/E 40–80x, then about 14 years to regain the index peak); real estate in 2007 (DLF and the realty index fell 80–90% and stayed down to ~2020); FMCG/consumer in 2019–21 (55–75x for HUL and Nestle, followed by roughly five years of flat-to-weak relative returns as multiples compressed); specialty chemicals at the 2021 China+1 peak (50–80x, then a 40–60% drawdown in many names through 2023–25 destocking); defence PSUs in 2023–25 (forward P/E ~2x historical); EMS in 2024–25 (60–120x). Common early signals at the top: the sector's P/E at more than 1.5–2x its own 10-year median, IPO and QIP supply surging in the theme, new entrants announcing capacity, and earnings upgrades slowing while prices still rise. Then a disclosure or accounting scare (Kaynes 2025) or a margin miss triggers the de-rating. Lesson: split past returns into earnings growth and multiple change, and assume the multiple mean-reverts over 5–10 years unless RoCE or growth has structurally changed. **lesson:** Decompose returns into EPS growth vs P/E change; a doubled multiple is a loan from future returns. **examples:** capital goods 2008; realty 2007; FMCG 2019–21; specialty chemicals 2021; defence 2024–25; EMS 2024–25 Sources: [1](https://www.businesstoday.in/markets/stocks/story/bel-hal-bdl-shares-targets-for-defence-stocks-after-rs-1-1-lakh-crore-dac-approvals-553813-2026-09-08) · [2](https://www.indexpe.in/blog/nifty-sector-valuations-june-2026) · [3](https://www.multibagg.ai/market-pulse/articles/dixon-q2-income-margin-drop-announcement-cmvv7szk200el2klzhj02h442) Links: illustrates `case_study:defence-psu-rerating`, illustrates `case_study:capital-goods-2007`, illustrates `case_study:kaynes-2025`, similar_to `insight:winners-drawdowns`

`strategy:arora-avoid-list` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: india, process, risk-management, growth

Rules (from his interviews): (1) Keep a sector avoid list - industries with chronically poor shareholder returns or governance (he has named PSUs, commodities, utilities, real estate among them at various times); excluding them cuts the error rate. (2) Diversify across ~30-40 growth stocks rather than a few bets. (3) Sell losers when the thesis is wrong instead of averaging down - he argues fewer than 5% of stocks are worth holding for the real long term, so long holding by itself is not an edge. (4) Let winners run. (5) Use macro judgment occasionally (raising cash in crises). Trade-off: avoid lists miss sector-wide rerating rallies (e.g., Indian PSUs 2021-24) - the cost of insurance against blow-ups. For an individual: write the avoid list down, define a review trigger for any stock down 25-30% from cost (re-underwrite, don't auto-average), and cap position size.

- Q3 FY27 revenue of about ₹347 cr (in line with Q1). Freight cost recovery in Q3.
- Ludhiana finishing shop rebuilt by 31-Dec-2026.
- FY27 revenue +24% (about ₹1,450 cr). EBITDA "comfortably above 20%". Working capital 136–140 days.
- Mexico: single-digit USD m in H2 FY27, with 2 of 3 customers still to ramp up.
- Capex of about ₹60 cr over the next year.
- Fabrication at 8–10% of revenue by about Nov-2028.
- Peak revenue (FY23 ₹1,366 cr) regained by FY27 or mid-FY28. TTM is already ₹1,346 cr.
- Long-dated items: ROCE ≥ 25% (re-derived TTM about 24.5%), share of >70 hp three-point linkage at 20–25% by FY30, ₹2,000 cr revenue in the "5-year plan", geographic mix 40/30/25/5.

**Practical read.** Treat the revenue and margin guide in this upturn as a floor. Push any strategic or timeline promise (Mexico, fabrication, acquisition) out by 1–3 quarters, and give the acquisition story no value until a deal is signed. Ask next time: (a) the FY26 small-ag growth number; (b) the aftermarket ₹ figure each quarter; (c) Mexico revenue in ₹; (d) the fabrication ₹ figure and its OEM share.
